title: sDMD: Sinkhorn Distribution Matching Distillation

paper.title: sDMD: Sinkhorn Distribution Matching Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) distills multi-step diffusion models into few-step generators by minimizing reverse KL divergence.
Despite its strong performance, DMD guides samples by local density alone, which introduces two limitations: teacher scores can be unreliable in regions of low teacher density, and the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can collapse the student onto a subset of the teacher modes.
We first connect DMD to Wasserstein gradient flow, showing that its gradient follows from a fixed-point formulation with integral KL (IKL) as the energy functional.
This perspective motivates augmenting IKL with an optimal transport term that addresses these limitations by guiding outlier samples toward the target and promoting mode coverage.
We realize this term using Sinkhorn divergence estimated from finite batches.
In practice, however, errors in the estimated Sinkhorn velocity can perturb in-domain samples for which IKL guidance is already accurate.
To this end, we introduce sDMD , which adaptively activates the Sinkhorn correction based on discriminator outputs, focusing on outlier samples where IKL may be unreliable.
With 2–4 sampling steps on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image-20B, and Wan2.1-14B, sDMD outperforms distillation baselines on GenEval, DPG, WISE, and VBench while improving sample diversity over DMD2.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Teaser. 4-step generated images using sDMD with FLUX.1 and Qwen-Image. Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) generate high-quality images and videos but require many sampling steps. Diffusion distillation reduces this cost by transferring knowledge from a pretrained teacher to a student that generates samples in one or a few steps. Existing approaches have advanced few-step generation by learning mappings along teacher trajectories ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2023 ) , using adversarial supervision ( Sauer et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) , or directly matching student and teacher distributions ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . Among these, a representative approach is DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ) , which optimizes a reverse KL objective using the difference between teacher and student scores. It has been widely adopted due to its high sample fidelity and scalability in large-scale image and video generation ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Ge et al., 2025 ) . To better understand and improve the training dynamics of DMD, we view diffusion distillation from the perspective of Wasserstein gradient flow (WGF) ( Ambrosio et al., 2008 ) . WGF evolves a probability distribution by steepest descent of an energy functional in Wasserstein space, with the corresponding velocity field specifying the update direction for each sample. While recent works ( Han et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) use WGF to train one-step generators from scratch, we establish its connection to diffusion distillation by recovering the DMD gradient through fixed-point regression under the integral KL (IKL) energy, defined as reverse KL averaged over diffusion noise levels ( Sec. 4.1 ). This identifies the energy underlying DMD and the velocity field that guides generated samples, allowing us to analyze the behavior and limitations of DMD and explore complementary energy functionals to improve distillation. The IKL velocity of DMD reveals two practical limitations ( Fig. 2 ). First, learned teacher scores can be unreliable for outlier samples, and the resulting updates may fail to guide them toward target modes. Although adding diffusion noise can improve distributional overlap, outliers may remain poorly supported at low noise levels. Higher noise levels can improve their support but blur the local structure of target modes. Second, the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can concentrate the student on a subset of target modes, potentially reducing the diversity of generated samples. To address these limitations, we augment IKL with an optimal transport (OT) term. OT couples student and target samples globally, providing robust guidance for outlier samples and promoting mode coverage without relying on learned teacher scores. To exploit their complementary strengths, we propose combining global OT guidance with local IKL score updates that help capture fine details. Our analysis shows that sufficiently strong exact OT regularization ensures convergence of the combined flow to the target under regularity assumptions ( Sec. 4.2 ). For efficient computation, we use Sinkhorn divergence, a debiased form of entropic OT. While Sinkhorn does not automatically inherit this guarantee, we establish sufficient conditions on its approximation error and regularization strength for the combined flow to converge to the target ( Sec. 5 ). In practice, the transport maps used to compute Sinkhorn updates are estimated from finite samples, with larger batches generally reducing estimation error at greater computational cost ( Genevay et al., 2019 ) . Notably, our experiments show that even with relatively few samples, Sinkhorn can provide more informative guidance than IKL for outlier samples where learned teacher scores are unreliable. However, for well-supported samples, estimation errors in Sinkhorn can instead interfere with the accurate guidance already provided by IKL. To this end, we introduce sDMD , which adaptively activates Sinkhorn guidance for samples with relatively weak teacher support based on discriminator outputs. We reuse the discriminator trained for adversarial regularization in DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) , without training a separate model. We evaluate sDMD using 2–4 sampling steps on FLUX.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) and Qwen-Image-20B ( Wu et al., 2025 ) for text-to-image generation ( Fig. 1 ) and Wan2.1 ( Wan et al., 2025 ) (1.3B and 14B) for text-to-video generation. sDMD outperforms the distillation baselines in most metrics on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , DPG ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , and WISE ( Niu et al., 2025 ) , achieves the highest overall VBench scores on both Wan2.1 models, and improves all reported diversity metrics over the strong DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) baseline.

sections.heading: Diffusion Distillation.
sections.text: To reduce the sampling cost of multi-step diffusion models, trajectory-based distillation methods enable one or few-step generation by learning shortcuts along denoising trajectories ( Song et al., 2023 ; Boffi et al., 2025 ; Frans et al., 2025 ) . Continuous-time formulations use JVPs ( Lu & Song, 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) , whose efficient computation at scale requires specialized implementations ( Zheng et al., 2026b ) . Recent works aim to avoid JVP computation through specialized architectures that decouple sampling substeps from backbone evaluations ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Shaul et al., 2026 ) . Adversarial approaches use discriminator-based supervision for distillation ( Sauer et al., 2023 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) with potential training instability ( Lin et al., 2025 ) . Distribution-matching distillation methods align generated and target distributions through f f -divergence minimization ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) or score matching ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) . Among these, DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Luo et al., 2023 ) minimizes the reverse KL divergence using the difference between teacher and student scores. With their high sample fidelity and scalability, DMD-based methods have been widely adopted for high-resolution image synthesis and video generation ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Yin et al., 2024a ) . However, DMD remains sensitive to outliers and the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL ( Bai et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Our work augments DMD with a complementary velocity field to address these limitations and improve sample quality and diversity.

sections.heading: Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Generative Modeling.
sections.text: WGF ( Jordan et al., 1998 ; Ambrosio et al., 2008 ) evolves a probability distribution by steepest descent of an energy functional under the 2-Wasserstein metric. When a divergence to the target distribution is chosen as the energy, the flow reduces the discrepancy between the two distributions, providing a framework for generative modeling. For example, MMD flows ( Arbel et al., 2019 ) depend on kernel gradients and can provide weak guidance when generated and target samples are far apart relative to the kernel bandwidth. This requires careful kernel design, such as noise-adaptive kernels ( Galashov et al., 2025 ) or kernels built from multiple feature encoders and scales ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . Sinkhorn divergence provides transport-based guidance ( Genevay et al., 2018 ; Feydy et al., 2019 ) , and recent works ( Han et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) use its gradient flow to train one-step generators. However, estimating transport from finite batches can introduce error into the resulting velocity field ( Pooladian & Niles-Weed, 2021 ; Genevay et al., 2019 ) . Flows based on reverse KL between clean distributions use local score information to guide samples toward the target distribution ( Li et al., 2023 ; Liu, 2017 ; He et al., 2025 ) . However, these approaches require known target densities or score estimates obtained through methods such as kernel density estimation, which can limit scalability in high-dimensional generation ( He et al., 2025 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, DMD offers a scalable diffusion distillation approach by applying reverse KL to noise-perturbed distributions with noise annealing. In this work, we connect DMD to WGF and propose sDMD , which incorporates an optimal transport term to improve guidance for outlier samples and promote mode coverage.

sections.heading: Connection to Prior and Concurrent Work.
sections.text: Diff-Instruct ( Luo et al., 2023 ) derives the generator score-difference update directly from IKL, but does not explicitly connect it to WGF. ProlificDreamer ( Wang et al., 2023b ) derives a WGF update for text-to-3D particles, but does not consider distillation into few-step image or video generators. Concurrent analyses ( Gretton et al., 2026 ; Turan et al., 2026 ) study WGF fixed-point regression for drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) using kernel-smoothed KL rather than IKL, and also do not explicitly connect DMD to WGF. In this work, we connect DMD to WGF under diffusion-noise-averaged KL from fixed-point regression and use this interpretation to introduce complementary Sinkhorn guidance for diffusion distillation.

sections.heading: 4.2 Limitations of IKL
sections.text: DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ) and its follow-up methods Fan et al. (2026) ; Ge et al. (2025) have demonstrated empirical success in capturing fine details and scaling to high-resolution image generation ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2024a ) and video generation ( Gu et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . However, the gradient of IKL in DMD guides particles by local density alone, which brings two practical limitations. First, the clean reverse KL gradient flow is ill-defined when p p and q q are mutually singular ( Glaser et al., 2021 ) . Although forward diffusion gives p t p_{t} and q t q_{t} full support, in practice the learned teacher score may remain unreliable for generated samples with low teacher density, particularly at low noise levels. Second, the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can cause the student to cover only a subset of the teacher modes. We illustrate these limitations using an experiment with a 2D Gaussian mixture ( Fig. 2 ). When the two distributions are well aligned, the predicted score is accurate and the particles converge onto the target ( Fig. 2 (a)). However, when a generated sample lies in a low-density region of the teacher distribution, the predicted score becomes inaccurate, and the resulting velocity fails to carry the particles toward the target under weak diffusion annealing ( Fig. 2 (b)). With higher noise levels, the sample can be better supported, but the velocity can ignore the local structure of the target distribution, and the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can collapse the particles onto a single mode ( Fig. 2 (c)).

sections.heading: Convergence with Exact OT.
sections.text: These limitations motivate augmenting IKL with an optimal transport (OT) regularizer. We show that IKL alone does not guarantee convergence from arbitrary initializations, whereas the WGF of exact OT contracts toward the target. Under regularity assumptions, a sufficiently strong exact OT term counteracts the negative curvature of IKL and ensures convergence of the combined flow to the target in Wasserstein distance ( Theorem 1 ). We provide a failure case for IKL and a sufficient condition on the OT regularization strength for convergence in Sec. B.2 . In the next section, we introduce a practical transport correction that complements IKL.

sections.heading: 5.1 Complementing IKL with Sinkhorn Divergence
sections.text: Despite the favorable convergence properties of exact OT, it can be computationally prohibitive. Instead, we use Sinkhorn divergence, a computationally tractable, debiased form of entropic OT with more favorable sample complexity ( Cuturi, 2013 ; Genevay et al., 2019 ) . We compare this choice with other energy functionals, including forward KL and MMD, in Sec. 6.3 . IKL and Sinkhorn induce complementary velocity fields that are useful in different regimes. IKL captures fine details through local score guidance in regions well supported by the teacher, whereas Sinkhorn uses a global transport plan to guide particles with weak teacher support toward the target and promote mode coverage ( Fig. 2 (d)). sections.heading: Convergence with Sinkhorn.
sections.text: We note that Sinkhorn does not automatically inherit the convergence guarantees of exact OT. However, under the assumptions in Sec. B.4 , a sufficiently large transport weight and a suitable bound on the Sinkhorn approximation error show convergence of the combined IKL and Sinkhorn flow to the target ( Theorem 2 ). Empirically, sDMD-U benefits from the complementary guidance of IKL and Sinkhorn. As shown by the blue box in Fig. 2 (d), Sinkhorn provides more informative guidance than IKL for outliers. In practice, however, the transport plan is computed on finite batches of student and teacher samples, which introduces error in the resulting velocity ( Genevay et al., 2019 ; Pooladian & Niles-Weed, 2021 ) . As a result, applying Sinkhorn at every iteration can perturb well-supported samples for which IKL already provides reliable guidance, as highlighted by the red boxes in Fig. 2 (d), while adding computational cost. We therefore seek a criterion that adaptively activates the Sinkhorn correction for samples with relatively weak teacher support, for which IKL guidance may be unreliable.

During training, the few-step generator produces oversmoothed or distorted samples that are outside the typical regions of the target distribution. sections.heading: Choice of Transport Space.
sections.text: The transport in Eq. 6 is computed on the sampled latents x ∈ ℝ d x\in\mathbb{R}^{d} of the student and the teacher. Instead, it can be computed in a feature space given a network ψ : ℝ d → ℝ n \psi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} , replacing the samples with the feature vectors ψ ⁡ ( x ) ∈ ℝ n \psi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n} . We empirically find that Sinkhorn transport computed in the clean latent space already provides effective guidance for outlier samples, avoiding the additional cost of a feature encoder. With this choice, sDMD incurs only marginal computational overhead compared with DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) . We present an ablation of the transport space and an analysis of computational cost in Sec. 6.3 and Appendix E , respectively.

sections.heading: Conditional Generation.
sections.text: For conditional generation, we compute Sinkhorn transport between M q M_{q} student samples and M p M_{p} teacher samples generated under the same conditioning input. To reduce training cost, we pre-generate the teacher samples for each conditioning input and store them in a buffer. While previous works applied Sinkhorn divergence to class-conditioned generation ( Han et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) , we extend its use to text-conditioned generation.

Tab. 4 evaluates the effects of the transport space and the gated Sinkhorn scheduler on sDMD . Applying Sinkhorn at every iteration (ungated) yields worse performance with more computational overhead. Finite-sample Sinkhorn errors can disrupt reliable IKL guidance ( Sec. 5.1 ), motivating our gated scheduler to activate transport only for samples with weak teacher support. However, feature-space transport requires additional forward passes and backpropagation through the feature encoder, whereas clean-latent transport offers competitive quality at a lower computational cost. We therefore compute the Sinkhorn transport in the clean latent space for the large scale generative models ( Wan et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) to balance sample quality and computational cost.

As shown in Tab. 5 , sDMD achieves higher scores than DMD2 on all reported diversity metrics across applications. sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we proposed sDMD , a diffusion distillation method that combines local score guidance of DMD with global transport. We first connected DMD to WGF by showing that the fixed-point relation with IKL as the energy functional recovers the DMD gradient. This connection enabled us to explore energy functionals that address unreliable guidance for outliers and limited mode coverage in DMD. Specifically, we augmented IKL with Sinkhorn divergence and introduced an adaptive scheduler to focus transport guidance on samples with relatively weak teacher support. Experiments showed that sDMD improves sample quality and diversity over strong diffusion distillation baselines in image and video generation with only marginal training overhead than DMD2. We discuss limitations and future work in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Comparison with Concurrent and Previous Works.
sections.text: DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ) uses diffusion-perturbed scores to approximate the clean reverse KL gradient, without an explicit connection to WGF. Diff-Instruct ( Luo et al., 2023 ) derives the IKL gradient for generator training without connecting it to WGF. ProlificDreamer ( Wang et al., 2023b ) derives a WGF update for 3D particles through a renderer, without considering fixed-point regression. While concurrent works ( Gretton et al., 2026 ; Turan et al., 2026 ) analyze kernel-smoothed KL and fixed-point training for drifting models, they do not explicitly study IKL averaged over diffusion noise levels or its connection to DMD. We focus on diffusion distillation with pretrained teacher scores, recovering the widely used DMD update through fixed-point regression under the IKL energy. This WGF perspective provides a common framework for deriving and combining velocity fields from complementary energy functionals to address the limitations of DMD in few-step image and video generation.

sections.heading: B.5 Analysis of IKL and Sinkhorn Velocity
sections.text: Sec. 4.2 discusses two limitations of DMD: unreliable guidance for outlier samples and mode collapse. Outlier behavior depends on multiple factors and is difficult to characterize in general, and we present empirical observations in Figs. 2(b) and 2(d) . In this section, we present analysis on mode coverage behavior using the toy example of ( Gretton et al., 2026 ) . We compare IKL velocity of DMD with sDMD and show how adding Sinkhorn preserves a correction toward an underrepresented mode when IKL guidance vanishes. We assume exact scores and transport plans. The diffusion coefficients α t , σ t \alpha_{t},\sigma_{t} control the noise level, while β > 0 \beta>0 independently controls Sinkhorn regularization.

sections.heading: Improving DMD with Finite Sinkhorn Batches.
sections.text: These properties make Sinkhorn alone a natural candidate for distillation. Indeed, concurrent works demonstrate that Sinkhorn can train generators from scratch ( Han et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . However, our analysis assumes that p p and q q are known exactly, while training computes Sinkhorn from finite batches. Finite batches introduce estimation errors in the entropic transport cost and the barycentric maps used to compute the velocity ( Genevay et al., 2019 ; Pooladian & Niles-Weed, 2021 ) . Therefore, small transport batches can yield inaccurate Sinkhorn guidance. In our ablation, Sinkhorn alone underperforms IKL ( Tab. 3 ). Nevertheless, combining Sinkhorn with IKL improves generation quality even with relatively small transport batches ( Tab. 9 ). We interpret this improvement in terms of their complementary roles: despite its own estimation error, Sinkhorn can provide more informative guidance than IKL for outlier samples, while IKL captures fine details in regions well supported by the teacher ( Fig. 2(d) ).

sections.heading: Training Few-Step Generators from Scratch.
sections.text: Recent methods train one- or few-step generators directly from data ( Song et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Boffi et al., 2025 ) , with often using JVPs during training ( Lu & Song, 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . Further advances improve stability and sample quality through revised objectives and training strategies ( Song & Dhariwal, 2024 ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and reduce computation costs through finite-difference approximations ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . On the other hand, recent methods use mini-batch particle interactions to align generated and target distributions during training ( Han et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . Our work distills few-step image and video generators from pretrained multi-step diffusion models widely used in real-world applications ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2025 ; Labs, 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Generative Modeling.
sections.text: WGF evolves probability distributions by steepest descent of an energy functional under the 2-Wasserstein metric ( Ambrosio et al., 2008 ) . The Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto (JKO) scheme ( Jordan et al., 1998 ) approximates this flow by minimizing the energy functional at each step, with a squared 2-Wasserstein penalty that keeps the updated distribution close to the distribution from the preceding step. Neural implementations ( Mokrov et al., 2021 ; Fan et al., 2021 ) optimize a transport map at each JKO step which incur quadratic training cost in the number of JKO steps. More efficient formulations have been proposed ( Choi et al., 2024 ; Bonet et al., 2021 ) , but their evaluation does not extend to the scale and dimensionality of modern generative models. In this work, we apply the WGF framework to diffusion distillation, training few-step image and video generators from large pretrained diffusion teachers.

sections.heading: Distribution Matching Distillation.
sections.text: The high sample quality and scalability of DMD have led to broad adoption in high-resolution image synthesis ( Yin et al., 2024a ) , hybrid consistency training for image and video generation ( Zheng et al., 2026b ) , and autoregressive video generation ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . Recent advances further improve its training and sampling: SenseFlow ( Ge et al., 2025 ) introduces fake-score alignment, while Decoupled DMD ( Liu et al., 2026 ) uses separate noise schedules for CFG augmentation and distribution matching. Other methods improve few-step distillation by matching intermediate distributions along the denoising trajectory ( Luo et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) . Additionally, recent works combine DMD-based and trajectory-based training objectives for few-step generation ( Cheng et al., 2026 ; Nie et al., 2026b ; Gu et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, AMD ( Bai et al., 2026 ) shares our concern about unreliable teacher guidance, but uses reward scores as a diagnostic proxy to adapt distillation updates. We derive the DMD update from WGF under the IKL energy, opening a design space of energy functionals for improving distillation. sDMD builds on this formulation by adding complementary Sinkhorn transport to improve sample quality and diversity. Additionally, this transport correction may complement the above DMD training strategies which we leave to future work.

sections.heading: ImageNet-256.
sections.text: We distill the pretrained SiT-XL/2 teacher ( Ma et al., 2024 ) (675M) into a one-step, class-conditional generator at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. Training uses ImageNet-1K images ( Deng et al., 2009 ) encoded into 32 × 32 × 4 32\times 32\times 4 latents with a pretrained VAE ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . The data loader groups the batch on each GPU by class, and each transport problem uses 8 clean student samples and 8 clean target samples from the same class. We compute Sinkhorn transport using features from a frozen MAE encoder, following the latent feature extraction protocol of Deng et al. (2026) . Each GPU processes two prompts per batch, with M q = M p = 8 M_{q}=M_{p}=8 samples per prompt, and transport is computed independently for each prompt. For feature transport, we use a frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 backbone ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) with inputs at 224 × 224 224\times 224 resolution and extract activations from blocks 3, 6, 9, and 12 to construct a multiscale representation.

sections.heading: Distillation and Training from Scratch.
sections.text: Recent methods achieve high generation quality by training one-step generators from scratch ( Han et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . In our analysis, we observe that teacher pretraining followed by distillation still requires fewer GPU hours than training a model from scratch ( Han et al., 2026 ) ( Tab. 10 ). Additionally, advances in representation learning further accelerate convergence and improve generation quality of pretrained models ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ) , supporting for pretraining followed by distillation as an efficient practice.

sections.heading: Appendix F Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: For conditional generation, sDMD requires multiple teacher samples for each conditioning input to estimate Sinkhorn guidance. While our ablations show that relatively few samples suffice to provide effective guidance for outlier samples, generating these samples still adds computational costs. Additionally, although our gated Sinkhorn scheduler improves performance, it uses discriminator outputs as a proxy for identifying samples with relatively weak teacher support. Exploring more reliable criteria for identifying samples that benefit from Sinkhorn guidance remains an interesting direction for future work. Lastly, we compute transport in the clean latent space for video diffusion models to reduce computational overhead. Exploring video feature spaces that provide a favorable balance between sample quality and computational cost remains future work.

Despite its strong performance, DMD guides samples by local density alone, which introduces two limitations: teacher scores can be unreliable in regions of low teacher density, and the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can collapse the student onto a subset of the teacher modes. We first connect DMD to Wasserstein gradient flow, showing that its gradient follows from a fixed-point formulation with integral KL (IKL) as the energy functional. This perspective motivates augmenting IKL with an optimal transport term that addresses these limitations by guiding outlier samples toward the target and promoting mode coverage. We realize this term using Sinkhorn divergence estimated from finite batches. In practice, however, errors in the estimated Sinkhorn velocity can perturb in-domain samples for which IKL guidance is already accurate. To this end, we introduce sDMD , which adaptively activates the Sinkhorn correction based on discriminator outputs, focusing on outlier samples where IKL may be unreliable. With 2–4 sampling steps on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image-20B, and Wan2.1-14B, sDMD outperforms distillation baselines on GenEval, DPG, WISE, and VBench while improving sample diversity over DMD2. † † footnotetext: † Work done during the internship at Netflix. † † footnotetext: ‡ Corresponding authors. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Teaser. 4-step generated images using sDMD with FLUX.1 and Qwen-Image. Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) generate high-quality images and videos but require many sampling steps. Diffusion distillation reduces this cost by transferring knowledge from a pretrained teacher to a student that generates samples in one or a few steps. Existing approaches have advanced few-step generation by learning mappings along teacher trajectories ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2023 ) , using adversarial supervision ( Sauer et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) , or directly matching student and teacher distributions ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . Among these, a representative approach is DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ) , which optimizes a reverse KL objective using the difference between teacher and student scores. It has been widely adopted due to its high sample fidelity and scalability in large-scale image and video generation ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Ge et al., 2025 ) . To better understand and improve the training dynamics of DMD, we view diffusion distillation from the perspective of Wasserstein gradient flow (WGF) ( Ambrosio et al., 2008 ) . WGF evolves a probability distribution by steepest descent of an energy functional in Wasserstein space, with the corresponding velocity field specifying the update direction for each sample. While recent works ( Han et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) use WGF to train one-step generators from scratch, we establish its connection to diffusion distillation by recovering the DMD gradient through fixed-point regression under the integral KL (IKL) energy, defined as reverse KL averaged over diffusion noise levels ( Sec. 4.1 ). This identifies the energy underlying DMD and the velocity field that guides generated samples, allowing us to analyze the behavior and limitations of DMD and explore complementary energy functionals to improve distillation. The IKL velocity of DMD reveals two practical limitations ( Fig. 2 ). First, learned teacher scores can be unreliable for outlier samples, and the resulting updates may fail to guide them toward target modes. Although adding diffusion noise can improve distributional overlap, outliers may remain poorly supported at low noise levels. Higher noise levels can improve their support but blur the local structure of target modes. Second, the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can concentrate the student on a subset of target modes, potentially reducing the diversity of generated samples. To address these limitations, we augment IKL with an optimal transport (OT) term. OT couples student and target samples globally, providing robust guidance for outlier samples and promoting mode coverage without relying on learned teacher scores. To exploit their complementary strengths, we propose combining global OT guidance with local IKL score updates that help capture fine details. Our analysis shows that sufficiently strong exact OT regularization ensures convergence of the combined flow to the target under regularity assumptions ( Sec. 4.2 ). For efficient computation, we use Sinkhorn divergence, a debiased form of entropic OT. While Sinkhorn does not automatically inherit this guarantee, we establish sufficient conditions on its approximation error and regularization strength for the combined flow to converge to the target ( Sec. 5 ). In practice, the transport maps used to compute Sinkhorn updates are estimated from finite samples, with larger batches generally reducing estimation error at greater computational cost ( Genevay et al., 2019 ) . Notably, our experiments show that even with relatively few samples, Sinkhorn can provide more informative guidance than IKL for outlier samples where learned teacher scores are unreliable. However, for well-supported samples, estimation errors in Sinkhorn can instead interfere with the accurate guidance already provided by IKL. To this end, we introduce sDMD , which adaptively activates Sinkhorn guidance for samples with relatively weak teacher support based on discriminator outputs. We reuse the discriminator trained for adversarial regularization in DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) , without training a separate model. We evaluate sDMD using 2–4 sampling steps on FLUX.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) and Qwen-Image-20B ( Wu et al., 2025 ) for text-to-image generation ( Fig. 1 ) and Wan2.1 ( Wan et al., 2025 ) (1.3B and 14B) for text-to-video generation. sDMD outperforms the distillation baselines in most metrics on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , DPG ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , and WISE ( Niu et al., 2025 ) , achieves the highest overall VBench scores on both Wan2.1 models, and improves all reported diversity metrics over the strong DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) baseline. 2 Related Work Diffusion Distillation. To reduce the sampling cost of multi-step diffusion models, trajectory-based distillation methods enable one or few-step generation by learning shortcuts along denoising trajectories ( Song et al., 2023 ; Boffi et al., 2025 ; Frans et al., 2025 ) . Continuous-time formulations use JVPs ( Lu & Song, 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) , whose efficient computation at scale requires specialized implementations ( Zheng et al., 2026b ) . Recent works aim to avoid JVP computation through specialized architectures that decouple sampling substeps from backbone evaluations ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Shaul et al., 2026 ) . Adversarial approaches use discriminator-based supervision for distillation ( Sauer et al., 2023 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) with potential training instability ( Lin et al., 2025 ) . Distribution-matching distillation methods align generated and target distributions through f f -divergence minimization ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) or score matching ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) . Among these, DMD ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Luo et al., 2023 ) minimizes the reverse KL divergence using the difference between teacher and student scores. With their high sample fidelity and scalability, DMD-based methods have been widely adopted for high-resolution image synthesis and video generation ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Yin et al., 2024a ) . However, DMD remains sensitive to outliers and the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL ( Bai et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Our work augments DMD with a complementary velocity field to address these limitations and improve sample quality and diversity. Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Generative Modeling. WGF ( Jordan et al., 1998 ; Ambrosio et al., 2008 ) evolves a probability distribution by steepest descent of an energy functional under the 2-Wasserstein metric. When a divergence to the target distribution is chosen as the energy, the flow reduces the discrepancy between the two distributions, providing a framework for generative modeling. For example, MMD flows ( Arbel et al., 2019 ) depend on kernel gradients and can provide weak guidance when generated and target samples are far apart relative to the kernel bandwidth. This requires careful kernel design, such as noise-adaptive kernels ( Galashov et al., 2025 ) or kernels built from multiple feature encoders and scales ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . Sinkhorn divergence provides transport-based guidance ( Genevay et al., 2018 ; Feydy et al., 2019 ) , and recent works ( Han et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) use its gradient flow to train one-step generators. However, estimating transport from finite batches can introduce error into the resulting velocity field ( Pooladian & Niles-Weed, 2021 ; Genevay et al., 2019 ) . Flows based on reverse KL between clean distributions use local score information to guide samples toward the target distribution ( Li et al., 2023 ; Liu, 2017 ; He et al., 2025 ) . However, these approaches require known target densities or score estimates obtained through methods such as kernel density estimation, which can limit scalability in high-dimensional generation ( He et al., 2025 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, DMD offers a scalable diffusion distillation approach by applying reverse KL to noise-perturbed distributions with noise annealing. In this work, we connect DMD to WGF and propose sDMD , which incorporates an optimal transport term to improve guidance for outlier samples and promote mode coverage. 3 Preliminaries Problem Setup and Notation. (2026) ; Ge et al. (2025) have demonstrated empirical success in capturing fine details and scaling to high-resolution image generation ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2024a ) and video generation ( Gu et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . However, the gradient of IKL in DMD guides particles by local density alone, which brings two practical limitations. First, the clean reverse KL gradient flow is ill-defined when p p and q q are mutually singular ( Glaser et al., 2021 ) . Although forward diffusion gives p t p_{t} and q t q_{t} full support, in practice the learned teacher score may remain unreliable for generated samples with low teacher density, particularly at low noise levels. Second, the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can cause the student to cover only a subset of the teacher modes. We illustrate these limitations using an experiment with a 2D Gaussian mixture ( Fig. 2 ). When the two distributions are well aligned, the predicted score is accurate and the particles converge onto the target ( Fig. 2 (a)). However, when a generated sample lies in a low-density region of the teacher distribution, the predicted score becomes inaccurate, and the resulting velocity fails to carry the particles toward the target under weak diffusion annealing ( Fig. 2 (b)). With higher noise levels, the sample can be better supported, but the velocity can ignore the local structure of the target distribution, and the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can collapse the particles onto a single mode ( Fig. 2 (c)). Convergence with Exact OT. These limitations motivate augmenting IKL with an optimal transport (OT) regularizer. We show that IKL alone does not guarantee convergence from arbitrary initializations, whereas the WGF of exact OT contracts toward the target. Under regularity assumptions, a sufficiently strong exact OT term counteracts the negative curvature of IKL and ensures convergence of the combined flow to the target in Wasserstein distance ( Theorem 1 ). We provide a failure case for IKL and a sufficient condition on the OT regularization strength for convergence in Sec. B.2 .
